chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
title: Joe Garland takes over with strict rules and uniform changes
summary: Garland took over, posted uniform changes and made the reed section rehearse between shows; the band improved but the work felt like a factory.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well, two days later, he sent for us to come to rehearsal. Joe Garland's going to take over the band. Joe Garland? Man, he was the last one to come in here. And he's gonna take over? Well, I thought that was kind of funny, you know, the last man to come in the band. But I said didn't say nothin'. It's all right with me. I learned my lesson from the Blue Rhythm Band. It didn't make no difference to me what happened.

So anyway, Joe Garland, he was the boss from then on. And he started givin' out his rules and one-thing-and-another, and... Boy, the first thing he did was, he had directions written in the dressing room, like we was playin' theatres. We had two or three different uniforms, and he'd have all different combinations and one-thing-or-another. And he had written up in all the dressing rooms what you wear the next show, this-that-and-the-other, and you change this... And after the first show every day, the' reed section rehearses. We rehearsed in between shows. "Damn," I said, "this is worse than going to work in a damn factory." We come off the stage and we've got to go to rehearsal right away." Then we finish rehearsal, and we've got to look on
the bulletin board and see what we're wearing for the next show.

It was funny. We'd come up, and we had blue suits and white suits. Because we had combinations. We changed the pants and jackets. One time, the reed section came out there with all blue pants and white jackets on, and the brass section was just the opposite. Everything was all mixed up. See, they did that just for the devilment, you know. Boy, it was a grand mixup.

But see, Joe Garland, he was so...he wanted things to be just exactly right. And I must say, from the records that I heard that they made, you know, under him, they were very good records. Very good records. He'd mark your music where you're supposed to breathe at. You'd play so many bars and then you take a breath. All them little things. He has us phrasing together. So it sounded much better. It really did improve the band.

But who wants to go through all that hassle? And we're not making that kind of money. And who is getting the... Louis Armstrong is getting all the credit and the money. And he didn't even... It didn't make no difference to him one way or the other. He'd go out and blow his horn. He don't know what's goin' on! He didn't care. As long as his chops was all right, he didn't care about nothin' else. All
he cared about was his chops. Practice all the time, blowin' his horn. And that's all he cared about. The band, they had a hard time. But...
